title: The queue: one global order, filterable by kind
spec: ONE global ordered queue (queue_position), not per-genre queues — Evan's explicit choice. Drag to reorder, persisted immediately; reordering is stable and gap-tolerant. Filter chips for anime / movie / live-action narrow the VIEW without forking the order. A whole series is one row — no episode tracking, explicitly out of scope. 'Up next' is simply position 1. ACCEPT: dragging item 9 to position 2 persists across reload; filtering to anime and reordering within the filter does not corrupt the global order.

refine.evidence: Spec at .autodev/specs/T-7.md, 9 ACs. AC5 is the one that decides whether Evan's 'one global queue, organizable by genre' is real rather than nominal: filter to games, reorder two of them, clear the filter, and every NON-game title must have kept its relative position. A per-genre-queue implementation passes a naive reorder test and fails this one. AC6 forces the gap-exhaustion collision rather than waiting to meet it — the positions are gap-tolerant by design (T-4 appends max+10, T-6 prepends min-10), so adjacent neighbours with no integer between them is reachable, and the move must complete via renumbering rather than silently refuse. AC7 exists because a drag-only reorder is unusable without a mouse.

locate.evidence: LOCATE. Existing: GET /api/titles?status=queued orders by 'queue_position IS NULL, queue_position, added_at' (T-4); PATCH /api/titles/{id} already takes a sparse body and already implements move_to_top as MIN-10 (T-6) — the same arithmetic family this ticket generalises. base.css carries .chip with aria-pressed styling (T-4), .poster, .kind, and the motion tokens. The carousel reads the same ordered endpoint, so AC3 needs no new wiring — it is a consequence, and the test is to prove it rather than to build it. MISSING: no endpoint moves a title to an arbitrary position; PATCH's move_to_top is the only reordering that exists. RISKS: (1) computing a new position from the FILTERED neighbours is what makes AC5 pass — using the filtered INDEX instead would renumber across hidden rows and scramble them; (2) the midpoint of two adjacent integers does not exist, so AC6's renumber path is reachable and must be written now rather than discovered later; (3) rows carry a remove button from T-4's card markup — a drag must not fire it, the same drag-versus-click hazard that broke T-5's carousel until pointerdown captured the target.

plan.evidence: PLAN: (1) POST /api/titles/{id}/move taking {after_id, before_id} — the two NEIGHBOURS the title should land between, never an index; (2) position arithmetic: midpoint of the neighbours' global positions, and when no integer fits, renumber the whole queue to multiples of 10 inside the same transaction and retry once; (3) queue view with pointer-based row dragging, a live drop indicator, and Alt+Arrow keyboard moves; (4) filter chips driving the view only; (5) component classes into base.css. DECISIONS: the API takes NEIGHBOUR IDS rather than a target index, which is what makes AC5 correct by construction — the caller passes the visible neighbours, so a filtered drag lands between exactly those two and every hidden row keeps its position untouched. Renumbering happens inside the same transaction as the move so a crash cannot leave the queue half-renumbered. The row-drag reuses T-5's lesson: capture the pressed element at pointerdown and swallow the synthetic click past the movement threshold, so dragging a row never fires its remove button.

build.evidence: BUILT AND PROVEN — .autodev/evidence/T-7/build.md. AC5, the criterion that decides whether 'one global queue' is real: dragged a game to the top INSIDE the games filter, cleared the filter, and all 8 non-game titles kept their exact relative order while the games reordered as asked. AC3: the queue's first row and the carousel's first card are both NieR: Automata — one sequence, no second source of truth. AC2 order survived a reload. AC6 gap exhaustion forced by repeated inserts into one gap; renumber fired, positions came out strictly ascending and unique, nothing lost. AC7 Alt+ArrowUp moved Hollow Knight above Super Mario 64. AC8 tested at 1 title (Alt+Up is a harmless no-op; filtering to a kind it is not gives 'Nothing in game') and at 0 (empty state + CTA). AC9 zero colour literals, 15 token refs, rendered in both alternate skins. Zero pageerrors and console errors throughout. Bundle-grep check from T-6 applied and passed.

auto-review.evidence: REVIEWED — one real defect, found by forcing AC6 rather than waiting to meet it, fixed and re-verified. THE MIDPOINT COLLISION: the first implementation took BOTH neighbours from the caller and placed the title at their midpoint, so with rows at 5 and 10 every insert 'between them' computed 7 — four titles ended up sharing position 7 and their order fell back silently to added_at, meaning a title dropped at the top landed last. The renumber guard never fired because 7 genuinely does fit between 5 and 10; the guard was asking the wrong question. Fixed so only ONE bound comes from the caller and the other is read from the database as the row actually adjacent now, plus a second guard rejecting a target another row already occupies. Re-ran the identical failing sequence: every title landed directly after the row named, positions unique and ascending, renumber fired on exhaustion (5/7/10 -> 10/11/12/15/20/60). Design decision that held up under the bug: the API takes NEIGHBOUR IDS not an index, because an index is meaningless in a filtered view — index 0 of 'games' is not index 0 of the queue. That choice is why AC5 was correct by construction and the defect was merely arithmetic. Row dragging reuses T-5's lesson (capture the pressed element, ignore movement below a 6px threshold) so a drag never fires the row's Open button.
